title: The Feigned Retreats at Hastings
text:
On 14 October 1066 Duke William of Normandy faced King Harold of England on a ridge near Hastings. Harold's army, only weeks after defeating a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, formed a dense shield wall along the crest. The Normans, with archers, infantry and mounted knights, had to attack uphill.

The morning attacks failed. The English line held, and at one point the Norman left, made up largely of Bretons, broke and fled downhill, pursued by some of the English. A rumor spread that William had been killed. According to William of Poitiers, the duke's chaplain, he rode among his men, pushed back his helmet to show his face, and rallied them. The Normans turned on the English who had chased them down the slope and cut them down in the open.

William of Poitiers then reports that the Normans used this experience deliberately. Twice more they pretended to flee, drawing groups of Englishmen out of the shield wall to pursue them, then wheeled their horses and destroyed them. Each time the English line grew thinner. Late in the day, after hours of attack with archers and cavalry, the line finally gave way. Harold was killed, along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine, and the English army collapsed.

William was crowned king of England at Westminster on Christmas Day 1066.
lesson: A disciplined opponent can be beaten by tempting him to break his own formation. Do not let an apparent success pull you away from the position that protects you.
source: William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi; the Bayeux Tapestry
caveat: Historians debate whether the later feigned retreats were truly deliberate or a flattering interpretation of real routs.
place: Battle Abbey, Battle, East Sussex, England
